scopeReview: IMP-3.B.1–5: hearths, languages/families/dialects, toponyms and representations, religion origins, expansion/relocation, six official religion examples, ethnic cultures and gender-role transmission. Categories are broad AP conventions rather than universal membership rules.
varietyReview: One flow map, language classification table, separate-denominator bar chart and growth ledger. Other cases cover Sikh origins/diaspora, Buddhist networks, ethnic diaspora, official classifications, border mismatch, scale and evidence for gender-role transmission. Varied keys and all five skills.
repetitionReview: Distinct mechanisms and representations: residential carriers versus converts; ancestry versus religion; names versus households; births versus arrivals. One classification recall item supports the official six-example requirement; applied questions dominate. No exact repeated stem or copied provider content.
referenceNote: Primary course framework and original institutional/scholarly accounts checked. Synthetic maps, counts and classroom representations are original; factual classifications are identified as such. Research references remain QA-only, not additions to the approved student resource library. Automated review is not independent human review.

questions.correctOption: Relocation to Harbor, followed by expansion among residents at the destination.
questions.independentReview: Separated changes in residence from changes in adherence. The directed route ends at Harbor and the later local adoptions occur there; no evidence identifies a new belief system or a government hierarchy.

questions.correctOption: They share a broad ancestral family even though they belong to different branches.
questions.independentReview: Cross-checked English/Germanic, Spanish/Romance and Hindi/Indo-Aryan classifications against the primary scholarly Indo-European reference. Family descent does not establish modern mutual intelligibility or religious identity.

questions.correctOption: Place names can preserve earlier language influence after everyday language use changes.
questions.independentReview: Independently checked 70% uses a place-name denominator while 20% uses households; no joint distribution is supplied. Historical naming can outlast predominant spoken use and cannot identify an exclusive diffusion mechanism.

questions.correctOption: Conversions account for 30 of 60 additional adherents; arriving adherents account for 20.
questions.independentReview: Recomputed 100+10+20+30=160 and growth60; conversion30/60=0.5, arrival20/60=1/3. Births are not labeled conversions. Supplied zero departures/deaths avoids an unstated net-growth offset.

questions.correctOption: Punjab is the historical hearth; migration can carry the tradition to distant communities.
questions.independentReview: Verified the Punjab/Nanak origins and diaspora institution context against Harvard’s Pluralism Project. Did not assign the cross-border Punjab hearth exclusively to a modern nation or claim all Sikhs have the same migration history.

questions.correctOption: Travel of religious specialists and teaching to new followers can combine relocation and expansion.
questions.independentReview: Checked primary Smithsonian scholarship on Buddhist exchanges through Silk Road networks. The scenario does not assign a modern majority region as the original hearth or assume spread occurred through military conquest.

questions.correctOption: Relocation can create distant communities of an ethnic religion; the category is not an exceptionless rule about every person.
questions.independentReview: Checked official IMP-3.B.5 wording, which says generally rather than always. Diaspora is consistent with relocation; the item does not equate Judaism with a single nationality or forbid conversion.

Verified all six categories directly against IMP-3.B.4–5. In particular Sikhism remains a universalizing example under the official AP classification; concentration in Punjab does not change this expected curricular label.

questions.correctOption: Political boundaries and language relationships need not coincide.
questions.independentReview: Distinguished political membership, linguistic relatedness and local practice as separate dimensions. Both observed cases directly reject a one-state/one-language-family assumption without requiring contested real-world language-versus-dialect labels.

questions.correctOption: Subnational language distributions that retain minority groups rather than only national majorities.
questions.independentReview: Checked the inference against the map’s stated unit and majority-only classification. A national color cannot recover minority locations; finer spatial resolution also needs minority-inclusive attributes, not just smaller polygons.

questions.correctOption: Dated records show contact, teaching about the roles, and later adoption in the receiving community.
questions.independentReview: Compared evidence for mechanism and temporal order rather than assuming resemblance proves diffusion. The item treats roles as socially transmitted and variable, not biologically fixed or uniform across a religion.
